common_name: Mary Christian Camellia (Early-Blooming Light Pink Williamsii Hybrid)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in fall or spring into moist, well-drained, acidic soil enriched with pine bark or compost, siting in partial shade with protection from harsh winter wind so the earliest buds are not blasted before they open.

directions: Mary Christian is one of the first Camellia x williamsii hybrids to flower each season, often opening single, cup-shaped, light pink blooms in mid to late winter well ahead of most japonica cultivars. Its compact, upright, densely twiggy growth habit makes it a good fit for narrow side-yard borders or foundation plantings where a looser camellia would outgrow its space. Because it blooms so early, choose a site shielded from the coldest north or west exposure so a hard freeze does not brown the opening flowers, and keep roots mulched and evenly moist through the heat of summer to support strong bud set for the following winter.

common_name: Elsie Jury Camellia (Large Deep Pink New Zealand Williamsii Hybrid)

planting.note: Transplant in fall or spring into humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; the narrow upright habit suits a tight courtyard corner better than a wide bed.

directions: Bred by Les Jury in New Zealand, Elsie Jury carries unusually large, deep pink flowers midway between peony and anemone form, often five inches across, on a narrower and more upright plant than many of its williamsii siblings. The big flowers can weigh down thin new growth in exposed wind, so stake young plants their first couple of winters and site out of strong gusts. Feed lightly with an acid-forming shrub fertilizer after the main spring flush fades, and shear only to correct shape immediately after bloom so next year's flower buds are not removed.

common_name: Jury's Yellow Camellia (Pale Yellow Peony-Form Williamsii Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in acidic, well-drained soil with reliable afternoon shade, since the pale petals can bleach or scorch faster than deeper-colored camellias under strong sun.

directions: Jury's Yellow is prized for petals that shade from plump pink buds into one of the clearest yellow-white tones found in any camellia, arranged in a formal peony-like double from late winter into spring. The pale color reads best with a dark evergreen backdrop, so pair it with broadleaf evergreens rather than a bright wall. Keep it out of midday sun and reflected heat, which can fade or brown the delicate petals faster than on darker-flowered williamsii hybrids, and mulch heavily since the fibrous roots dislike drying out between waterings.

common_name: Saint Ewe Camellia (Long-Blooming Rose-Pink Caerhays Hybrid)

planting.note: Set out in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; give it room to arch outward since it grows wider and more informal than many compact williamsii cultivars.

directions: Raised at Caerhays Castle in Cornwall, Saint Ewe produces single, trumpet-shaped, rose-pink flowers over an unusually long season that can stretch from early winter well into mid-spring in mild climates. Its vigorous, somewhat arching growth is better suited to a woodland edge or mixed shrub border than a tightly clipped foundation hedge, so allow extra lateral space when siting it. Water deeply during dry spells in its first two years to establish a deep root system, after which it tolerates brief dry stretches better than many camellias, though consistent moisture still produces the heaviest bloom.

common_name: Debbie Camellia (Rosy Pink Long-Season New Zealand Williamsii Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; the dense habit takes well to light shaping as a specimen or informal screen.

directions: Another Les Jury introduction from New Zealand, Debbie bears peony-form, rosy pink flowers over a remarkably long window that runs from late winter into May in favorable climates, giving a bigger return than many camellias that finish blooming in a few weeks. Its dense, rounded habit holds shape well with minimal pruning, making it a reliable choice for a loose hedge or repeated specimen planting along a shaded path. Watch for the fibrous surface roots competing with nearby turf or groundcover, and keep a mulched root zone free of grass to reduce moisture stress during summer heat.

common_name: Plain Jane Camellia (Extra-Cold-Hardy White-Flowered Tea Oil Camellia)

planting.note: Plant in fall or spring in well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; this selection tolerates more open exposure and colder sites than most ornamental camellias.

directions: Plain Jane was selected from Camellia oleifera seedlings for even greater cold tolerance than the well-known 'Lu Shan Snow,' and breeders including Dr. William Ackerman have used it as parent stock for cold-hardy ornamental hybrids rather than growing it chiefly for its own display. Its single white flowers open in fall and are modest compared with showier japonica or williamsii cultivars, but the plant's tough, cinnamon-barked, upright habit and exceptional hardiness make it useful as a tall screening shrub in colder regions where other camellias fail. Give it an open site with good air movement and full sun exposure it would not tolerate as well in milder zones, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the current season's wood.
